items.title: A descent one fifth the height of the Great Pyramid
items.body: The three shafts sum to 30.37 m, about 21 percent of the Great Pyramid's original 146.6 m height; the section's deepest label, 35.45 m, is about 24 percent. At the bottom lies a hall of roughly 80 square metres with a 32 square metre island, all cut from living rock. The basalt sarcophagus there is 2.28 m long and 1.08 m wide, while Shaft C measures 1.65 x 1.90 m: the sarcophagus is 38 cm longer than the shaft's wider side, but narrower than either side, so it could in principle be lowered end-first. Hawass suggests that seven small niches cut into the walls of the niche at the head of Shaft C might have held wooden beams used to lower it.

items.title: The suppression story and the permit record
items.body: Hancock and Bauval's Keeper of Genesis (1996; US title The Message of the Sphinx) tells it as a pattern. Schoch's team had permission from the antiquities president, yet Hawass, they write, 'fell upon them, suddenly and unexpectedly, like the proverbial ton of bricks' and 'virtually thrown the American team off the site' (1993-94). They say the authorities halted Waseda's work at the Queen's Chamber of the Great Pyramid, that a 1995 West-Schoch application to resume research was ignored, and that Hawass said in July 1996 he had stopped the Schor-funded team. They also write that almost no further research had been officially authorized at the Sphinx since 1982. They present this as orthodoxy burying inconvenient evidence about what lies under the paws.
items.rebuttal: The record shows heavy permitted probing. SRI and RSI drilled in 1978, RSI arriving with a drill and 'official permits' per Hancock and Bauval, and Dolphin says the holes were drilled with permission from the Giza Inspectorate. Waseda sounded the Sphinx in 1987, an Egyptian team ran seismic refraction in 1992, Florida State's Schor expedition surveyed for three weeks in April 1996, and Hancock and Bauval themselves record approvals for 1991 and a one-year licence for 1996. Hawass's stated 1997 rule is no drilling into the Sphinx on anomalies alone. Friction was real: in a January 1994 press quote reproduced by the authors, Hawass called the endoscope filming by West's team unscientific. In 2018-19 Hawass and Lehner's own Return to the Sphinx Viewing Project had radar run on the Sphinx and Sphinx Temple area, though the one published result covers the terrace beside the Sphinx Temple. The 'since 1982' gap also rests on a project Lehner's letter, printed in the authors' appendix, says took place in 1978.

items.title: The 10,500 BC idea meets radiocarbon
items.body: From 1984 to 1995 archaeologists collected over 450 organic samples, mostly charcoal flecks in mortar and straw in mud brick, from Old and Middle Kingdom monuments including the Giza pyramids. The first project, in 1984, was backed by the Edgar Cayce Foundation, whose interest rested on Cayce's hypothesis that the Giza pyramids dated to 10,500 BC. Of that first project Bonani and colleagues write that the results confirmed the sequence of the monuments and their ages as historians set them, but that the match was only approximate and left open a difference between the two chronologies, so a second project began in 1995. A 2009 reanalysis found most Fourth Dynasty dates, from 158 measurements at 12 sites, ran 200 to 300 years older than expected, and a Bayesian outlier treatment pulled them much closer to the historical record.

items.title: Cleopatra, Khufu and the true size of 10,500 BC
items.body: Cleopatra VII died in 30 BC. Khufu's reign began about 2589 BC, which is 2,559 years earlier. The Moon landing was in AD 1969, 1,998 years later, since there is no year zero. Cleopatra therefore lived closer in time to Apollo 11 than to the Great Pyramid's builders, by about 560 years. Now stretch the ruler: 10,500 BC lies 7,911 years before Khufu, 1.7 times the 4,614 years from Khufu to 2026. Even Gobekli Tepe, whose mound began to build up about 9600 BC and whose earliest excavated enclosures date to roughly 9500 BC, predates Khufu by about 7,000 years, more than the whole span from Khufu to today.

items.title: Stone-age crowds moving multi-tonne stones
items.body: A 1963 survey noted Gobekli Tepe but took the pillar tops for grave markers. In October 1994 Klaus Schmidt recognized them as the tops of megaliths, and digging began in 1995. The monumental T-shaped pillars in the round enclosures stand up to about 4 m around an even larger central pair (about 5.5 m in Enclosure D), and more than 60 are known; geophysics suggests at least 20 enclosures. Dietrich and colleagues put the largest megaliths at up to 7 m, 50 metric tons and 20 cubic metres, five times the volume of a stone that 525 men hauled 3 km in three days on Nias; treat the 50 tonnes as their upper estimate for the biggest stones, not the weight of a typical erected pillar. The mound is 300 m wide and 15 m high, built before pottery, from about 9600 BC.

items.title: A comet, a catastrophe and a lost Ice Age culture
items.body: In 2007 Richard Firestone, Allen West and colleagues proposed in PNAS that one or more low-density objects exploded over northern North America about 12,900 years ago, partially destabilizing the Laurentide Ice Sheet, causing widespread biomass burning and triggering the Younger Dryas cooling and megafaunal losses. They describe a thin layer identified at about 50 Clovis-age sites and report in it magnetic grains, microspherules, charcoal, soot, nanodiamonds and fullerenes; a platinum spike in Greenland ice was added later. Graham Hancock links the event to a vanished Ice Age civilization and to flood myths. Sweatman and colleagues (2024) say supporting evidence now spans more than 50 sites on five continents.
items.rebuttal: Holliday and twelve co-authors (2023) find no crater of that age, markers with identification and interpretation problems, and no clear population or megafaunal collapse. Boslough and colleagues (2012) put the odds of the proposed comet configuration near one in 10 to the 15th. Green and colleagues (2025) place the platinum spike 45 to 50 years after the cooling began and favor an Icelandic fissure eruption, while not excluding an unknown meteorite. Mainstream explanations center on weakened Atlantic circulation.

items.title: The Vulture Stone as a record of the comet
items.body: In 2017 Martin Sweatman and Dimitrios Tsikritsis of the University of Edinburgh proposed that Gobekli Tepe's enclosures were observatories and that animal carvings are constellations. They single out Pillar 43, the Vulture Stone of Enclosure D, reading its scorpion as Scorpius, its outstretched-wing vulture as the Sagittarius teapot, and its headless man as death. They date it to 10950 BC plus or minus 250 as a stamp of the Younger Dryas comet, calling chance matches extremely remote. They accept a gap of about 1,000 years to the site's earliest radiocarbon date, suggesting the pillar predates the walls. Hancock's 2015 book had drawn a related date-stamp reading from Paul Burley.
items.rebuttal: The excavators (Notroff, Dietrich, Clare and colleagues) say the proposed date is 700 to 1,000 years older than the oldest radiocarbon date for Enclosure D, and the earliest site dates match the end of the Younger Dryas, not its onset. They doubt asterisms stay stable for millennia, note the headless figure's emphasised phallus, point to more than 60 pillars and site-wide iconography, and call the impact premise itself contested.

items.title: Alvarez 1968: the King's Chamber that was not there
items.body: Luis Alvarez's team installed spark-chamber muon detectors in Khafre's Belzoni Chamber in spring 1967 under the Joint U.A.R.-U.S.A. Pyramid Project, and recorded from early 1968. Partway through analysis a signal suggested a King's-Chamber-sized cavity about 30 m above the detector, with roughly a 10 percent count increase. It vanished once the apparatus and pyramid geometry were modelled exactly. They concluded they could have seen any chamber in their field of view, and found none. It stays a cautionary tale for any muon excess: statistics alone are not enough.

items.title: Giza's bedrock and the stone that travelled
items.body: The plateau is the Mokattam Formation, middle-Eocene limestone and dolomite laid down on the Tethys Sea floor. Fossil nummulite shells, about 50 million years old, still show in pyramid blocks, and most of the Great Pyramid's 2.3 million blocks were quarried just south of it. The Sphinx is cut from three Mokattam units tilted about 10 degrees southeast: hard reef rock at the base (the paws are cut from this lowest unit), alternating soft and hard layers in the body, harder stone in the head. Most of the stone was local; the premium stone travelled: white Tura limestone across the Nile, and about 8,000 tonnes of granite from Aswan, 800 to 900 km upriver, a mere 0.13 percent of the mass.

items.title: Diary of Merer: a 4,500-year-old logbook from a Red Sea harbour
items.body: In 2013 Pierre Tallet's French mission excavated hundreds of papyrus fragments at the mouth of a storage gallery at Wadi el-Jarf, a Red Sea harbour. Tallet publishes them as the oldest papyrus archive found in Egypt, from the end of Khufu's reign. The best-preserved logbooks follow Inspector Merer and a crew Tallet estimates at about 40 boatmen (inferred partly from a monthly bread ration), shipping Tura limestone toward Akhet-Khufu, on average two or three round trips every ten days, most likely from July to November of the year after the 13th census (Year 26). Tallet judges the stone was most probably, though not exclusively, for the pyramid's exterior casing; the logbook itself does not say what the blocks were for. Ankhhaf, Khufu's half-brother and vizier, controlled the Ro-She Khufu staging post. Tallet's own extrapolation, which assumes a boat carrying about 30 blocks of 2.5 tonnes (the real load is unknown), is about 200 blocks a month and 1,000 in a season, a tiny share of the 2.3 million blocks.

items.title: Tallest human-made structure for more than 3,700 years
items.body: At 146.6 m the Great Pyramid was the tallest human-made structure from about 2600 BC. The end date depends on which medieval spire you count, and Wikipedia's article text words it cautiously as 'more than 3,700 years'. Its infobox ends the reign in 1221 with Old St Paul's steeple, traditionally 149 m. Lincoln Cathedral's lead-clad spire, reputedly 160 m though some doubt it, took the title in 1311. Counting from 2600 BC gives 3,820 years to 1221 and 3,910 years to 1311, so 'about 3,800 years' is a fair round figure and 'more than 3,700' the safest. Both spire heights are disputed, and Christopher Wren put St Paul's nearer 140 m, below the pyramid. Wikipedia's succession box also lists the disputed Yongning Pagoda (516 AD) as a possible earlier rival.

items.title: Five hectares of base and a block every few minutes
items.body: A 230.3 m square covers 53,038 square metres, 5.3 hectares or 13.1 acres. A FIFA-recommended 105 by 68 m pitch is 7,140 square metres, so the base holds about 7.4 pitches. Building 2.3 million blocks in about 26 years means roughly 242 blocks every day if work ran on every day of the year; over a 10-hour working day (both assumptions made for this page) that is one block set about every 2.5 minutes, and faster if there were rest days. Burgos and Laroze's 2020 quarry experiment, as reported on Wikipedia, extrapolated about 250 blocks a day from roughly 3,500 quarrymen.

items.title: Heit el-Ghurab: the bread and beef behind the pyramids
items.body: Since 1988 Lehner's AERA team has dug a purpose-built town of more than 7 hectares, about 400 m south of the Sphinx, with bakeries, kitchens, workshops and grain silos. Seven hectares is about ten pitches, consistent with Smithsonian's 'bigger than ten football fields'. Population estimates vary: Smithsonian says the barracks could have accommodated 1,600 to 2,000 workers, Hawass said in 2010 that about 10,000 labourers ate 21 cattle and 23 sheep daily, and a 1999 management study gave 13,200 on average and 40,000 at peak. Honoured burials beside the pyramids, work-gang graffiti and Merer's logbook all describe organised, fed crews. One caveat: AERA dates the town to the builders of Menkaure, Khafre and 'probably' Khufu, and Tallet doubts it is the Ro-She Khufu port in Merer's logbook.

items.title: Ancient astronauts and the 'impossible' pyramid
items.body: In Chariots of the Gods? (1968) and later books, Erich von Däniken argued that some ancient monuments, the Great Pyramid among them, were built by extraterrestrial visitors or by humans who learned the necessary knowledge from them. He described ancient Egypt as a 'fantastic, ready-made civilization' that appeared suddenly and without transitions. Supporters of the idea generally argue that the size of the stones and the precision with which they were laid exceed the tools of the time; the Great Pyramid's roughly 2.3 million blocks, aligned to within minutes of arc of true north, are the kind of figures this argument leans on.
items.rebuttal: The record shows a vast but human project. Pyramids develop over generations from mastabas through Djoser's step pyramid to Sneferu's true pyramids. Merer's logbook shows a crew Tallet estimates at about 40 men hauling Tura stone to Akhet-Khufu, work-gang graffiti naming Khufu survive in the relieving chambers, and bakeries, workers' tombs and a Khufu-era quarry with arsenical-copper chisels have been excavated. The scientific consensus is that the hypothesis is unjustified and unnecessary, and critics say it diminishes ancient peoples' achievements.

items.title: A passage found by an old man's memory, not by radar
items.body: In 1926 Emile Baraize's clearing of the Sphinx exposed an opening in the rump, which was later hidden again under restoration masonry. Mohammed Abd al-Mawgud Fayed had worked as a boy on that clearing and went on to serve about 40 years as an overseer of workmen and guards for the Antiquities Service. In 1980 he told Hawass and Lehner where to look, and Hawass had one brick-sized stone removed to check. Mohammed picked the right one: a crudely cut passage with cup-shaped footholds, one branch of which winds down to a dead end about 4.5 m below floor level (Wikipedia gives 5 m). Lehner stresses that memory found it, not remote sensing. From the 1926 clearing to the 1980 reopening is 54 years; Hawass says 'nearly half a century' and Lehner 'more than 50 years'. Hawass names Mohammed alone, while Wikipedia's summary says three elderly basket carriers recalled it, and who cut the shaft is debated.

items.title: Reading the Sphinx enclosure's weathering
items.body: The Sphinx is about 73 m long and 20 m high, carved from Eocene Mokattam Formation limestone whose layers differ in hardness: the softer middle body has decayed more than the harder head layer. Four mechanisms are argued. Schoch: rainfall running down the enclosure walls cut vertical fissures and undulating profiles. Harrell: burial in wet sand, tectonic joints widened by groundwater, and wear on the wall tops. Gauri and colleagues: salt crystallization driven by dew. Reader: run-off from occasional flash flooding, which he argues could place the carving some centuries before Khufu. Harrell writes that most of the weathering may have occurred during the roughly 1,100 years between Khafre's carving and Thutmose IV's encasement of the Sphinx, around 1400 BC.

items.title: A Sphinx older than the pharaohs
items.body: In the 1950s Rene Schwaller de Lubicz proposed that the Sphinx's body had been eroded by deluges, and John Anthony West carried the idea to geologist Robert Schoch, who presented it in 1991. In their telling, the enclosure walls show vertical fissures and undulating vertical profiles that only prolonged rainfall can make, while wind makes horizontal bands, and Egypt's last significant rainfall ended between the late fourth and early third millennium BC, before the Old Kingdom. So the Sphinx must be older. Schoch's dates moved: before 5000 BC at first, later a minimum of 9700 BC. He and West add that other Giza surfaces and early Saqqara mudbrick tombs lack similar wear.
items.rebuttal: Lehner puts an earlier builder civilization at a very, very low level of probability and ties the Sphinx to Khafre's complex. Harrell attributes the wear to wet sand, tectonic joints and about 1,100 years of exposure before Thutmose IV. Gauri and colleagues favor dew-driven salt crystallization. Hawass cites poor limestone, and Welc and Marks suggest heavy rainfall continued to about 2200 BC. Reader finds runoff erosion but argues the carving predates Khufu, and now places it in the Second Dynasty, not 10,000 BC.

items.title: The Leo alignment and the First Time
items.body: Hancock and Bauval hold that Giza was designed to lock the date 10,500 BC, Zep Tepi. Precession, they say, had brought the Age of Leo, which Hancock reckons at roughly 10,970 to 8810 BC, and at dawn on the spring equinox the Sphinx looked directly at Leo and the Sun rising beneath it. The lion Sphinx, the Belt-pyramids and the Nile-Milky Way pairing then read as one sky map of that moment. Earlier, Edgar Cayce had also placed the Giza pyramids at 10,500 BC, a hypothesis that the foundation bearing his name helped fund radiocarbon tests of.
items.rebuttal: The astronomy is real but the reading is not forced. By a computation made for this page the equinox point at 10,500 BC sat near Denebola, Leo's tail, 21 degrees past Regulus and 33 short of Spica, so Fairall's Virgo and Hancock's Leo both lean on where modern boundaries fall. Krupp notes Egypt had no zodiac until Graeco-Roman times. The Cayce-backed radiocarbon tests gave ages near the historians' Fourth Dynasty dates, and papyri date work to Khufu's 27th year.

items.title: How the light was made: real Cycles bakes, not a painted gradient
items.body: The surface shading is not a hand-made gradient. Blender's Cycles path tracer lit the pyramids, Sphinx, causeway and ground once per time of day, sun plus a physical sky, with real cast shadows and real bounce light, and each result was stored as vertex colour. The page swaps between the stored sets, so moving the light slider costs nothing at run time. The trade is that the light is fixed to those states: the X-ray and layer sliders do not re-light anything, and the starlight state is the albedo dimmed to a blue night tone, not a bake.

items.title: The sun walks straight down the lion's gaze
items.body: The Sphinx faces due east, so on the equinoxes the sun rises exactly along its line of sight. Choose Equinox sunrise: the light comes in low (the baked sun is 7 degrees up, about half an hour after sunrise at Giza's latitude), and at that angle a 20 m lion throws a shadow more than 160 m long, back across the enclosure toward the pyramids. The builders did not need a calendar to know the sun's path; the stone does it for them.

He credits Georges Castel of the French Institute in Cairo with mapping the architecture of the tomb.

items.title: Who found it, and when
items.body: Selim Hassan described the shaft from his sixth season (1934-35 by inference), published in 1944; he found its lowest level flooded and could not pump it down. Hawass writes that in 1945 Abdel Moneim Abu Bakr learned guides were swimming in it, but never excavated or published it. Hawass began digging in summer 1999, using pumps supplied by Esmail Osman, divers sent in before draining, and plaster on wall cracks as movement warnings. A section label records a water level dated 20 November 1997. Deseret News carried a Reuters report of the sarcophagus on 16 February 2000.

items.title: Dating: sherds, sarcophagus styles and a place-name
items.body: Hawass reasons in layers. The earliest finds are Sixth Dynasty potsherds in Shaft C, so he argues the shaft was first cut then (c. 2345-2181 BC). The Level 3 sarcophagus is 26th Dynasty by style (664-525 BC); Level 2 sarcophagi and shabtis are mostly 26th Dynasty; scarabs and djed amulets are Late Period. He cites a New Kingdom place-name, House of Osiris, Lord of Rostau, for reuse, but describes no New Kingdom object. Hassan called such deep shafts Saitic. A 2000 Reuters report gave 500 BC and also New Kingdom, which cannot both hold.
items.topic: The Osiris Shaft at Giza

items.title: One hole, three deep layers of time
items.body: If the Sixth Dynasty potsherds mark the first cutting (c. 2345-2181 BC) and the burials Hawass dates are 26th Dynasty (664-525 BC), then 1,500 to 1,800 years of Egyptian history separate the shaft's first cutting from those burials. Herodotus, who visited in the 5th century BC, would already have been looking back about 1,700 to 1,900 years at the earliest sherds, taking 450 BC. From the Saite burials to the pumps of Hawass's 1999 dig is another 2,500 to 2,700 years. One hole, three deep time layers.

items.title: A swimming hole above the 'tomb of Osiris'
items.body: Before it was fully excavated, the shaft already had a modern life. Hassan reported ice-cold water, analysed as pure, which his whole staff drank, a luxury he called perhaps unique in a desert site. Hawass writes that guides swam in it each summer, that workmen at Cairo University's rest house ran a pipeline to it, and that it became a centre of New Age rumour about tunnels. Through all of this a basalt sarcophagus waited in the dark, in a water-ringed hall about 30 m down.

items.title: The actual tomb of Osiris?
items.body: Hawass's reading: the complex is a dummy tomb for the god Osiris, cut in the Sixth Dynasty as the Osiris cult rose, and reused in the New Kingdom, when he says Giza was known as the House of Osiris, Lord of Rostau. He sees a sarcophagus on a pillared island ringed by water, echoing the Osireion at Abydos, with four pillars as the god's sacred legs, and matches the setting to Herodotus's island tomb fed by a canal. He also cites the Inventory Stele, which places the house of Isis northwest of the house of Osiris.
items.rebuttal: These are interpretations. Hawass's list of finds (amulets, scarabs, a bead, sherds) includes no inscription naming the shaft, though he does report two schist amulets in the form of Osiris from the tomb. Herodotus ascribed his island chambers to Khufu, not Osiris, and Hawass himself notes that Herodotus probably did not enter the shaft and relied on guides. Hawass reports a skeleton in the Level 3 sarcophagus, so it was not an empty dummy when found, and dates the tomb to the Late Period from scarabs and djed amulets found on the north side of the chamber (not in situ). A 2000 Archaeology magazine summary reports the Herodotus match as a claim in media reports and says a visit to the tomb 'calls into question both its interpretation and its history of exploration'. Hassan, writing in 1944, classed it as the most striking example of an abnormally deep Saitic shaft tomb.

items.title: Hidden tunnels to the Sphinx and Great Pyramid
items.body: Before 1999 the flooded shaft fed stories of tunnels to the Sphinx and Great Pyramid, which Hawass says New Age circles spread. Hancock and Bauval's 1996 book relays Jean Kerisel's suggestion that the Sphinx may stand over the entrance to a 700 m tunnel leading to the Great Pyramid, once filled or partially filled with water. A blog compiling accounts around the late Boris Said's 1997 radio interview reports 1996 radar results from the Schor-Said survey that seemed to show a tunnel about 2 m wide and 3 m below the surface running west from the Sphinx's tail under the causeway, and says Said's team later recorded a domed anomaly about 2.5 m wide sloping about 25 degrees toward the Sphinx.
items.rebuttal: Hawass's component list for the excavated complex is Shafts A to C and Chambers A to I, and he describes no passage leading out; he presents the tunnel talk as rumour. Kerisel's tunnel is a hypothesis, and Hancock and Bauval themselves pose it as a question. The radar claims are secondhand, from a blog relaying a radio interview and survey accounts, and no published survey linking any tunnel to this shaft was found.

items.title: Rostau, the Kingdom of Osiris and a water road
items.body: In The Message of the Sphinx (1996), Hancock and Bauval argue that Rostau, an ancient name for Giza, was also the Kingdom of Osiris, reached by two roads, one by land and one by water. They read the Book of What is in the Duat as showing a water-filled tunnel under a Sphinx's paws, and cite Dobecki's rectangular cavity about 9 by 12 m, less than 5 m down, plus a water table about 10 m below the Sphinx floor. The book predates the 1999 dig; no text by either author treating the excavated shaft as confirmation was found.
items.rebuttal: The shaft lies under Khafre's causeway, not the Sphinx's paws. Hawass argues his Osiris reading from Rostau place-names, Pyramid Texts, the Osireion parallel and general New Kingdom Netherworld texts; he does not cite the Book of What is in the Duat or treat it as a map of Giza. He attributes the shaft's water to a high water table, and Hassan could not pump it down. Dobecki's cavity is a seismic inference; nothing opened for this page shows it was excavated. And the book itself notes that Egyptologists do not dispute that the Rostau of the ground is the Giza Pyramid-field, so a subterranean Osiris realm rests on interpretation.

items.title: The unopened sarcophagus and the mysteriously rising water
items.body: An Ancient Origins article published in September 2018 gives a first-person account of a visit earlier that year. It describes the lowest chamber as flooded since at least 1934, says the water had risen higher than expected that year, and says the authorities do not know its source. It reports a stone-slab-covered sarcophagus, with carved lines on the slab, just beneath the water, which a Giza inspector confirmed had never been opened. It cites the visitor's own lab test as showing salty water, points to Lake Moeris and the Hawara Labyrinth, citing Herodotus on 'pathways' between Hawara and Giza, and speculates about a network of tunnels and waterways. In that telling the Osiris Shaft is the visible doorway to a vast hidden watery network beneath Egypt.
items.rebuttal: Hawass reports that the lid (268 x 108 x 35 cm) lay on the floor of Shaft C and that a skeleton lay in the sarcophagus, so it was evidently opened before his team moved the lid over it; the slab the visitor saw may be that repositioned lid. Hassan found the level flooded in the 1930s and four years of pumping failed, and Hawass blames a high water table, so rising water needs no hidden source. Hassan also reported having the water analysed and finding it pure enough to drink, whereas the article's salinity claim rests on one lab test by the visitor. nothing excavated or published was found that supports a link to Hawara, and Hawass's text describes no tunnel opening from Chamber I.

items.title: What the 1992 seismic paper actually says
items.body: Thomas Dobecki and Robert Schoch published "Seismic investigations in the vicinity of the great Sphinx of Giza, Egypt" in Geoarchaeology 7(6), December 1992, pages 527-544. Fieldwork combined seismic refraction, refraction tomography and high-resolution reflection inside the Sphinx Enclosure, at the Sphinx Temple, and in desert to the east and south. The abstract reports uneven weathering below the enclosure floor, a series of cavities on each side of the Sphinx and between its paws, and sand-buried bedrock showing excavated or possibly downfaulted structures. It states no chamber size, no depth and no single paw. The full text could not be opened for this page.

items.title: SRI at the Sphinx, 1977 and 1978: anomalies drilled, nothing found
items.body: SRI International's 1977 resistivity survey, as quoted from its report by Hancock and Bauval, flagged a possible northwest-southeast tunnel behind the rear paws and two deep anomalies in front of the paws. In 1978 the follow-up used resistivity (Lambert Dolphin's later comment lists 1 m spacing plus 2, 4, 8 and 16 m on a switch box, though his main text recalls one-foot spacing), a seismic sounder with a useful range of 125 to 150 ft, and a borehole TV camera. Five 4-inch holes, three in the temple area and two in the platform, showed minor natural cracks and, in Lehner's words as quoted by Hancock and Bauval, 'Swiss-cheese-like solution cavities'. Dolphin's team concluded there were no major rooms, voids or filled cavities. Caveats: Dolphin says no formal 1978 report was ever written and the resistivity logs cannot be found; Lehner counts three anomalies drilled, Dolphin five holes; and Lehner recalls that on the last days of SRI's 1978 fieldwork an acoustic test on the bedrock floor went dead at three spots that were never checked.

items.title: A 2019 radar look beside the Sphinx Temple
items.body: In 2018 and 2019 Hawass and Lehner's Return to the Sphinx Viewing Project set out to collect 45 years of Sphinx investigations, much of it unpublished, and add new radar. In March 2019 the Glen Dash team ran a 500 MHz pulseEKKO survey near the Sphinx Temple, with stations every 0.25 m. It found a uniform reflection about 1 m down, consistent with levelling blocks, and narrow right-angle reflections to about 4 m, read as buried support blocks rather than a tunnel. 1980 cores show bedrock dropping 12 m further east. The authors say only direct observation can confirm it. The results published in this article cover the area beside the Sphinx Temple, not the Sphinx's own floor.

items.title: How big is the lion, and how small is the anomaly?
items.body: Scale makes the search feel enormous and tiny at once. The Sphinx is about 73 m long, 20 m high and 19 m wide, carved from the plateau's own limestone. SRI's seismic sounder had a useful range of roughly 125 to 150 ft, which is 38 to 46 m, or 52 to 63 percent of the animal's length. Dobecki described the much-quoted 1991 seismic feature as about 9 by 12 m, 108 square metres, 'buried less than five metres in depth'. Read as depth to its top, that is under a quarter of the Sphinx's height, and its footprint is about one-thirteenth of the 73 by 19 m rectangle bounding the whole statue. Hancock and Bauval elsewhere put the same chamber about twenty feet (about 6 m) down, roughly 30 percent of the Sphinx's height, so even that depth is not settled.

items.title: The 9 by 12 metre chamber under the paws
items.body: In April 1991 geophysicist Thomas Dobecki's seismic lines, run for Schoch's survey, picked up cavities between and beside the Sphinx's paws. On NBC's 1993 Mystery of the Sphinx he described one as about nine by twelve metres, buried less than five metres down, with a regular rectangular shape he said was hard to square with nature, so possibly man-made. Presenter Charlton Heston added that it lay where Cayce said, under the front paws. Hancock and Bauval later called it a large chamber in the bedrock.
items.rebuttal: The 1992 abstract reports only cavities on each side and between the paws, with no size and no claim of a room. Lehner stresses that an anomaly is a data feature needing interpretation, and Sphinx limestone holds natural solution cavities and a huge fissure. A 1992 Egyptian seismic refraction study found four rock layers and no cavities. No record of drilling to test the feature was found. Note that 5 m is burial depth, not a third dimension, that Hancock and Bauval's Chapter 12 instead says about twenty feet (about 6 m), and that Hawass and Schoch place it at the left paw.

items.title: The "one system" idea: everything is connected underground
items.body: In popular retellings the Hall of Records under the paw, the Osiris Shaft, the Great Pyramid's chambers and the deep shafts claimed under Khafre are parts of one planned underground complex, joined by tunnels, with Herodotus's account of a tomb on an island ringed by Nile water as supporting colour. The glowing network on this page draws that idea, with three pulses travelling along it.

items.rebuttal: The network is the page's own illustration of the claim, not a map of anything. The excavators describe the Osiris Shaft as a closed three-level complex reached from above, not a junction; the 1991 survey's anomaly has never been drilled or opened; the Great Pyramid's void is measured inside the pyramid; the Khafre claim is unpublished. Each of the five places is a separate question with a separate evidence file, and joining them multiplies unknowns instead of adding support. Herodotus's island tomb (2.124) is a report about Khufu's tomb heard from priests, which the Osiris Level 3 island chamber resembles, but resemblance is not a link. Treat the glowing lines as a picture of the question 'what if', not of an answer.

items.title: A medieval treasure guide older than Cayce
items.body: Treasure lore about the Sphinx is older than Cayce. Jason Colavito points to a late medieval Arabic treasure-hunters' guide, the Kitab al-durr al-maknuz ('Buried Pearls'), in Ahmed Bay Kamal's two-volume 1907 French translation, section 309. In Colavito's own translation it tells the seeker to measure seven cubits from the back of the neck and dig to three times the height of a man, which he glosses as about 18 ft. Two large slabs enclose an entrance leading by corridor to a large door and a large room with four hundred cells full of silver. Eighteen feet is 5.5 m, near the 5 m scale of the modern seismic claim, but a neck is not a paw: a coincidence of scale, not a match.

items.title: The believer who went to look
items.body: The Egyptologist who mapped the Sphinx began among the Cayce believers. His parents introduced him to Cayce's writings (Smithsonian), and in 1974 he published, through A.R.E. Press, a book drawn from about 300 of 1,159 Cayce readings on Ra-Ta, saying 'the final confirmation lies beneath the paws of the Sphinx at Giza'. Hancock and Bauval reproduce his letter of 16 Nov 1995: he says he already had doubts when he reached Egypt in 1973 but hoped evidence could be found, read Festinger's When Prophecy Fails in 1974, and found tool marks, names and skeletons of people instead of footprints of gods. Of his mid-1970s remark that the Hall of Records was worth looking for, he wrote 'but not in a tangible way. You know, like the Holy Grail.' He adds that the negative SRI results of 1977-78 and Old Kingdom deposits near the paws 'sealed it' for him that Cayce's story had an extremely low probability of reflecting real events.

items.title: Cayce's readings: a record chamber at the right forepaw
items.body: Edgar Cayce, the Virginia Beach trance clairvoyant, said Atlantean refugees stored their records in a hall near the Sphinx. Reading 5748-6, which Hancock and Bauval date to 1 July 1932, speaks of 'a chamber or passage from the right forepaw to this entrance of the record chamber'. Reading 378-16 says the sunrise line of shadow or light falls between the paws and, as quoted on an A.R.E.-hosted page, that a sealed room reached from the Sphinx's right paw 'may not be entered ... until the TIME has been fulfilled'. Followers place the hall between the Sphinx and the river, dated near 10,500 BC. Hancock and Bauval report that the readings were taken to point to its opening in 1996 to 1998 (elsewhere 'perhaps in 1998').
items.rebuttal: No sealed room or record chamber matching the readings has been found, and the A.R.E.-hosted page 'Our Research into Cayce's Hall of Records' claims no discovery. SRI's five 1978 boreholes met natural cavities. The one rump passage ends in a dead end about 4.5 m down, with modern debris near its base. Lehner, once in the Cayce circle, wrote in 1995 that he had urged the Cayce community to see the Egypt and Atlantis story as myth, and that the SRI results and Old Kingdom finds convinced him it was very unlikely to be literally true. The 1996 to 1998 window has passed. The official reading transcripts could not be viewed.

items.title: The Halls of Amenti: a different hidden hall
items.body: In Maurice Doreal's Emerald Tablets of Thoth the Atlantean, Thoth is a deathless Atlantean priest-king who ruled Egypt from about 52,000 to 36,000 BC. Leaving, the preface says, he raised the Great Pyramid over the entrance to the Great Halls of Amenti and hid his records there under chosen guards. Tablet II sings of halls deep in Earth's heart, far beneath the islands of sunken Atlantis, where 32 Children of Light dwell. The preface says Doreal was instructed to recover the tablets (kept by the Maya in Yucatan) and return them to the Great Pyramid, and was allowed to translate and keep a copy, which 'was done in 1925'; Wikipedia summarises the claim as tablets found in the Great Pyramid in 1925.
items.rebuttal: No record was found of the tablets ever being produced for examination, and the preface itself says they were returned to the Great Pyramid. Wikipedia classes the book as pseudohistory and dates its first publication to the 1940s or early 1950s, most likely before 1953, so it appeared well after Cayce's early-1930s Hall of Records readings; some bibliographic listings give 1930, which could not be verified. Wikipedia says Doreal was inspired by Lovecraftian fiction, naming 'The Dunwich Horror' (Lovecraft, 1928) and 'The Hounds of Tindalos' (1929, by the Lovecraft-circle writer Frank Belknap Long). The text puts the entrance under the Great Pyramid, not the Sphinx, and a reign from 52,000 BC with Thoth as builder of the Great Pyramid contradicts the Egyptological dating of the Giza monuments to about 2500 BC. The Cayce and Doreal traditions are distinct.

items.title: Khafre's 648 m shafts: a claim read from satellite radar
items.body: In March 2025, at a press conference in Italy, Filippo Biondi and Corrado Malanga said satellite synthetic aperture radar, processed with what they call Doppler tomography, revealed structures beneath Khafre's pyramid: five connected structures above the shafts, eight vertical cylinders wrapped by spiral pathways reaching about 648 m, and two cube-shaped structures reported at about 90 m a side. Coverage also cites a deeper complex near 2 km and, per National Geographic, an age near 38,000 years. Supporters say the method does not need radar to penetrate rock; it reads sub-millimetre ground vibrations. Armando Mei, quoted by TRT World, cites 200-plus tomographies and satellite data from two American aerospace companies.
items.rebuttal: ESA says radar penetration is limited, to about 10 m at best, and Biondi himself says under 10 m; 648 m is 65 times that. Sarah Parcak says SAR data cannot see through rock, and Flint Dibble cites about 2 m; Lawrence Conyers called the vast-city claims a huge exaggeration. Zahi Hawass calls the claim baseless and, per National Geographic, says no permit was granted. Nothing is peer-reviewed, and National Geographic says the reconstructions appear AI-generated. The team's 2022 Khufu paper was retracted in August 2026 for methodological flaws and statistical errors; the notice did not allege fabrication or research misconduct, and the authors disagreed (Parcak's remark that they willfully misinterpreted the data is her opinion, not a journal finding). The retraction does not rule on the Khafre claims, and the coverage read for this page reports no fieldwork test of them.

items.title: How well do we know when Khufu reigned?
items.body: Egyptologists tabulate Khufu at about 2589 to 2566 BC, while the von Beckerath lower range Kate Spence used starts him at 2554 BC. His reign ran 23 years on the Turin list, with a highest known year of 28 or 29. Radiocarbon dating (211 measurements on short-lived plants, by Bronk Ramsey and colleagues) puts the start of Djoser's reign, in the Third Dynasty, between 2691 and 2625 BC. Spence assumes pyramids were aligned in a king's second year and models two drifting circumpolar stars; she recalibrates Khufu's accession to 2480 BC, plus or minus 5. Papyri from Wadi al-Jarf date work to his 27th year. The live debate spans about a century, not 8,000 years.

items.title: Big Void: three instruments, one hollow above the Grand Gallery

KEK scintillator hodoscopes in the same chamber confirmed it, and CEA Micromegas gas detectors outside the north face re-confirmed it. items.title: North Face Corridor: a 9 m void sized by muons
items.body: Published in Nature Communications on 2 March 2023 (Procureur and 35 co-authors), the paper pins down a corridor-shaped void behind the chevron stones above the original entrance. Two independent analyses, Nagoya emulsions (2019 data) and CEA gas telescopes (installed October 2019), both favour a horizontal void about 9 m long and roughly 2 m by 2 m. Nagoya puts its north end about 0.84 m behind the chevron; CEA's less precise figure is 0.45 +/- 0.22 m, and the paper rounds to 0.8 m. The excess was above 10 sigma in both analyses. The paper does not establish a function, saying only that the larger cross-section may be decisive in approaching the role of the chevron. Sharing the raw data needs Egyptian antiquities ministry approval.

items.title: Particles from space as an X-ray for stone
items.body: Cosmic rays strike the upper atmosphere and rain muons on Earth at roughly 10,000 per square metre per minute, about one per square centimetre per minute. Through a pyramid only around 1 percent arrive. Dividing the Nagoya film counts by exposure gives about 99,800 tracks per square metre per day, roughly 0.7 percent of the surface rate, a calculation made for this page but in line with that 1 percent. A hollow shows up as a few percent extra muons, 5 to 11 percent in the KEK slices. A 5.8 sigma excess is about a 1 in 300 million fluke, counting statistics only.

items.title: The room left unfinished beneath the pyramid
items.body: Far below the finished King's and Queen's Chambers, a rough-cut room sits in bedrock at the end of a long descending passage, its western half only trenched and left jagged. Why? Borchardt thought it was the first burial chamber, abandoned when plans changed. Stadelmann argued it was cut last, halted by Khufu's death, a symbolic underworld. Lehner reasoned the King's Chamber was planned early because Petrie found the sarcophagus too wide for its door. In 1837 Vyse and Perring's workers sank a shaft in its floor, about 15 m deep on Wikipedia's account, with the Nile's then water level a further 12 m down, and found no further chamber.

items.title: The cedar plank rediscovered after 148 years
items.body: In 1872 engineer Waynman Dixon opened the Queen's Chamber shafts by chiselling through the chamber wall and recovered a ball, a hook and a piece of cedar. The ball and hook went to the British Museum; the wood went to Scotland, was donated to the University of Aberdeen in 1946 and was misfiled. In 2020, 148 years after Dixon's find, curatorial assistant Abeer Eladany found it in a cigar box. Radiocarbon places it at 3341 to 3094 BC, roughly 500 to 800 years older than the pyramid. Aberdeen's Neil Curtis offered two readings: the date reflects the heartwood of a long-lived tree, or scarce cedar was treasured and reused. So the date applies to the wood, not necessarily to the pyramid.

items.title: Giza as a power plant: the Queen's Chamber electrodes
items.body: Christopher Dunn's Giza Power Plant theory treats the Great Pyramid as a machine. On his account, the southern Queen's Chamber shaft delivered dilute hydrochloric acid and the northern shaft a zinc solution, producing hydrogen, with the metal fittings on the shaft slabs acting as electrodes. He cites erosion on the southern shaft floor, a white deposit on one northern fitting read as electroplating, and the Pyramid Rover's ultrasonic slab thickness of 3.25 inches against his illustrated 3.64 inches, which he presents as a successful prediction.
items.rebuttal: By Dunn's own page, the 3.64 inch figure was arbitrary (he also calls it a vindicated prediction), so it cannot count as a test, and he concedes there are no clear images of the back of the southern slab. Gantenbrink's survey describes simple fittings, probably cold-forged and bent down at 90 degrees, with a black tarry substance at the drill-hole openings and gypsum-like white marks on the stone and fittings. Per Wikipedia, the Djedi team in 2011 believes the handles were decorative and found the back of the door finished and polished. A false door or ritual barrier, as Stadelmann proposed, needs no chemistry, and no survey report opened for this page describes plant remains.

items.title: Were the narrow shafts aimed at the stars?
items.body: In the 1960s Alexandre Badawy proposed that the King's Chamber southern shaft pointed to Orion's Belt, and Virginia Trimble that the northern shaft pointed to the northern circumpolar stars, the Indestructibles. Later accounts list Alpha Draconis, Sirius and Beta Ursae Minoris around 2500 BC as targets, reading the shafts as launch paths for the king's soul, with Orion as Osiris and Sirius as Isis. In this telling the shafts are deliberate aiming lines tying the dead king to the stars.
items.rebuttal: Large stones block the shaft exits and the shafts have horizontal sections, so they could not be used to sight stars, and the shafts were only roughly oriented. The Queen's shafts were found sealed, blocked at both ends, when Dixon opened them in 1872, and the northern one bends sharply at 18 m, which leaves no line of sight (an inference). A ritual passage for the king's soul needs no sighting. Leeds' Rob Richardson says that, given the artwork found in the southern shaft, it is likely the shaft served a bigger purpose than ventilation; the question is unresolved.

items.body: Writers such as Scott Creighton, in a 2021 author feature on Graham Hancock's site for his book The Great Pyramid Void Enigma, present the Big Void as a massive, previously unknown space about as large as the Grand Gallery, possibly a hidden chamber, one that 'seemingly came from nowhere'. He leans on three independently working teams, on ScanPyramids co-director Mehdi Tayoubi, whom the feature quotes as saying the structure was carefully planned and is not an irregularity of construction, and on 2019 follow-up scans he says put it near 40 m long. The feature does not allege a cover-up.
items.rebuttal: Muons measure missing density, not purpose or contents. The original paper leaves open one or several structures, horizontal or inclined, and none of the sources opened for this page reports direct inspection, so every explanation remains untested. Zahi Hawass said in November 2017 that the pyramid is full of voids and this is not a secret chamber or a discovery, and Wikipedia says he speculates it may be a gap used in building the Grand Gallery; the Japanese team says it differs from previously identified construction spaces. The antiquities council head said findings should be discussed before announcement. The 40 m figure appears only in the author's own feature; it could not be verified.

items.title: How close to true north? About 3 arcminutes
items.body: Petrie's 1880s theodolite survey and Nell and Ruggles' 2006 total-station survey agree that the Great Pyramid's sides are turned slightly counterclockwise from true north. Nell and Ruggles put the casing-foundation edges at 3.6, 3.4, 0.5 and 3.7 arcminutes (north, east, south, west) with accuracy near 1 arcminute. Petrie's casing-base figures averaged 3 minutes 43 seconds, while his rougher core masonry averaged 5 minutes 16 seconds. The 3 minutes 38 seconds quoted on Wikipedia is Glen Dash's 2012 average, derived from the 1984 Lehner-Goodman survey data rather than from a new survey. Over a 230.3 m side, 3.6 arcminutes is only about 24 cm of sideways drift. So 'about 3 arcminutes' is fair, but the honest range is roughly 0.5 to 5.

items.title: Casing stones and their hair-line joints
items.body: The pyramid was finished in white Tura limestone. The lowest course is the tallest at 1.49 m; upper courses are close to one cubit, with stones near 500 kg, and about 203 courses remain. Edwards (1986) reported casing and chamber joints averaging only 0.5 mm, and Petrie in 1883 called the pavement, lower casing and entrance passage exquisitely wrought, saying the means of placing and cementing blocks with such hair-like joints was almost inconceivable at present. Unfinished casing at the Menkaure and Henutsen pyramids suggests faces were smoothed after the stones were set, using chiselled seams as guides. Most of the casing was stripped in the Middle Ages (one tradition names 1356). The pyramid is about 8.1 m shorter than its design height, a loss shared between the stripped casing, the lost pyramidion and stones taken from the peak.

items.title: Khufu's cedar boat, sealed beside the pyramid
items.body: In 1954 Kamal el-Mallakh found a boat pit sealed into Giza bedrock beside the pyramid. The ship inside, rebuilt from 1,224 pieces, is largely Lebanon cedar, built shell-first with planks lashed by halfah grass and a flat bottom with no true keel. Its length is quoted as 43.4 m (Wikipedia), 143 ft or about 43.6 m (one maritime outlet) and 42 m or 138 ft (Egyptian-ministry-based news reports from 2021); beam is 5.9 m. At 43.4 m it is about 1.45 blue whales long. A Djedefre cartouche on the pit's cover blocks suggests his son sealed it. It reached the Grand Egyptian Museum in 2021 after a 48-hour move.

items.title: Too precise for copper tools? The lost-machining claim
items.body: Manufacturing technologist Christopher Dunn argues that Giza's granite shows machine-grade work: flat surfaces checked with a steel straightedge, uniform corner radii, saw grooves about 0.05 inch apart on the King's Chamber coffer, a spiral groove in Petrie's drill cores that he reads as a feed rate about 500 times that of modern diamond drilling, and lathe-like marks on diorite bowls. Such feed rates, he says, rule out copper tools with sand, so he proposes advanced machining and calls ultrasonic machining the only method that fully satisfies the technical logic. He writes 'I am not an Egyptologist. I am a technologist,' and his essay is a personal account built on his own visits, instruments and Petrie's data, with no experimental test of the ultrasonic proposal and no peer-reviewed analysis.
items.rebuttal: Giza's precision is real but uneven. Petrie (1883) praised the pavement and lower casing, yet found the Grand Gallery's upper ramp tilted more than an inch across 20 inches, and core blocks are only roughly dressed. Stocks's 2003 experiments suggest the surfaces could have been prepared with simple rods and string, with mud and gypsum reducing friction when blocks were moved and fitted; his abstract frames the target as flatness to about a hundredth of an inch. A NOVA test cut a hole in a granite slab with a sand-fed copper pipe on a bow drill, though it gave no rate. Glen Dash's replication of Petrie's pole-star method erred by about 1 arcminute per sighting. Fine tool-mark questions remain debated.

items.title: Is pi built into the Great Pyramid?
items.body: Proponents note that the base perimeter (4 x 440 = 1,760 cubits) divided by the height (280 cubits) is 6.2857, within 0.04 percent of 2 pi, 6.2832. Petrie judged such circle relations systematic enough to be design, and Verner wrote that the Egyptians used pi in practice though they could not define it. In the popular version the Great Pyramid is a stone book of mathematics, deliberately encoded for the future.
items.rebuttal: A slope of 5.5 palms per cubit (14 up, 11 across) forces the ratio: 1,760 / 280 = 44/7, exactly twice 22/7, with no knowledge of pi needed. Other scholars argue Egyptians had no concept of pi to encode. The match is also finer than the data: surveyed side lengths differ by 0.20 m (0.09 percent), and the 146.6 m height comes from a design of 280 cubits, since the apex is missing, so 0.04 percent cannot be resolved.

items.title: Zep Tepi and the 10,500 BC claim
items.body: Hancock and Bauval build on Zep Tepi, the First Time, which they present as the Egyptians' memory of a real epoch when Osiris brought civilisation. They tie it to the sky of 10,500 BC, the age of Leo, when they say Orion's Belt matched the three Giza pyramids, making the Sphinx a Leo marker and Giza a star map. The same date appears in Cayce's readings. Hancock and Bauval say they offer no opinion on the merits of Cayce's information, but describe the Hall of Records as an older hidden-chamber tradition that has become entangled with Giza research; no passage was found in which they propose locating a hall by reading the plateau as a sky template.
items.rebuttal: In Egyptian texts zp tpj, the first time, denotes the moment of transition from primordial chaos to the existing world (Assmann 1994, via Wikipedia), a cosmological reading that Hancock and Bauval turn into history. Sources for Egyptian creation myths date to the Old Kingdom, about 2700 to 2200 BC, and the Edfu temple texts sit in a building raised 237 to 57 BC. Astronomer Tony Fairall says the Orion alignment misses by more than five degrees, and BBC Horizon (1999, revised and rebroadcast in 2000) argued that with enough points you can find almost any pattern. A 2014 surface luminescence study dated the Sphinx and Valley temples to the middle to late third millennium BC.

items.title: The precession clock: one lap takes about 25,772 years
items.body: Earth's axis wobbles like a spinning top, and the equinox point slides westward along the ecliptic at about 50.29 arcseconds a year. One lap takes about 25,772 years by Wikipedia's figure; some sources use 25,771.4. Because the motion is smooth and well measured, any sky can be run backwards. A star's declination changes, the pole star changes, and the spring equinox drifts through the zodiac: Taurus around 2500 BC, and by a computation made for this page near the Leo-Virgo junction around 10,500 BC. Over 12,500 years the equinox covers 48.5 percent of a lap, about 175 degrees by simple linear arithmetic or about 171 degrees from a long-term precession model.

items.title: Checking the Belt against the plateau
items.body: Take the standard mapping: Alnitak is the Great Pyramid, Alnilam is Khafre's, Mintaka is Menkaure's. On the ground, Khufu to Menkaure runs about 37 degrees west of south over roughly 930 m, from Wikipedia coordinates, close to the 38 usually quoted. In the sky at 10,500 BC the Mintaka-to-Alnitak line stood about 50 degrees from vertical as the Belt crossed the meridian, at the top of Krupp and Fairall's 47 to 50; the angle shifts by nearly a degree per century of epoch, so 'about 50' is the honest precision. Today it is about 53. The sky and ground angles therefore differ by about 12 to 13 degrees before the orientation dispute even starts. Legon also gives figures that, by the same scale, put the extended Abu Roash and Zawiyet el-Aryan mapping off by 'nearly twice' and 'less than half' (ratios of about 1.9 and 2.6 computed from his numbers).

items.title: The Belt that barely cleared the horizon
items.body: From Giza, a star crossing the southern meridian peaks at 90 degrees minus the gap between the observer's latitude and the star's declination. Alnilam, the middle Belt star, sits at declination minus 1.2 degrees today and peaks near 59 degrees. By 2500 BC precession had moved it to minus 14.8 and it peaked near 45; Alnitak peaked near 45.0, the same angle as the King's Chamber south shaft. At 10,500 BC the declination was about minus 50 degrees and the whole Belt crept only about 10 degrees above the southern horizon, close to its lowest point in the entire 25,772-year cycle.

items.title: A sky that changes its pole star
items.body: Precession also drags the celestial pole across the stars. Thuban in Draco was the pole star from 3942 to 1793 BC and passed within 10 arcminutes of the pole around 2830 BC, over two centuries before the Great Pyramid rose. Vega, the brightest of the successive pole stars, held that role around 12,000 BC within about 4.5 degrees of the pole, and returns around AD 13,724. Polaris, about a degree off the pole now, comes back around AD 27,800. In Spence's model the builders reached their famous north alignment, off by only a few arcminutes on the Great Pyramid, by watching two circumpolar stars cross together.

items.title: Giza as a map of Orion's Belt
items.body: Robert Bauval, first in Discussions in Egyptology 13 (1989) and then with Adrian Gilbert in The Orion Mystery (1994), argues that the three great pyramids are a ground plan of Orion's Belt, the sky-image of Osiris. In this account Alnitak is Khufu's pyramid, Alnilam is Khafre's, and Mintaka, the faintest and westernmost star, is the smaller, slightly offset Menkaure. The Nile mirrors the Milky Way. Graham Hancock and Bauval add that the plan locks in 10,500 BC, which they call Zep Tepi, the First Time. Answering the charge that the map is upside down, Hancock says that standing north of the pyramids and looking south toward Orion shows the Belt as the pyramids lay it out, and Bauval says an audience's drawings of the Belt matched the Giza plan.
items.rebuttal: Krupp and Fairall measured the Belt's tilt in that era at 47 to 50 degrees against the pyramids' 38, and a computation made for this page gives about 50, at the top of their range. Krupp says a match needs one pattern inverted. Legon adds that the Belt stars look nearly equal while the Third Pyramid has about a tenth of the Great Pyramid's volume, and that the extended mapping fails on scale. The UK Broadcasting Standards Commission ruled for the makers of the BBC programme Atlantis Reborn on all but one of Hancock's and Bauval's ten principal complaints; the one it upheld was that the programme omitted their rebuttal of a specific argument against the Orion correlation.

items.title: How the sky was made: catalogue, frame, precession
items.body: The page reuses the star catalogue from the x3d-blender-io demo page: 978 stars from the HYG database, the real directions of the neighbours within 50 light-years. Those are a faint, true-direction field, not the naked-eye sky, so 41 bright named stars (Orion, Leo, the Plough, Sirius, Arcturus and others) were added from Sesame coordinates, with stick figures for three constellations. The catalogue frame was matched to the sky with one rotation fitted on Sirius and Procyon, and eleven other named stars land within 0.16 degrees of where they should. Precession uses the long-term Vondrak model in 100-year steps from 13,000 BC to 2100 AD; alt-azimuth follows from Giza's latitude and the sidereal hour you set. Proper motion is ignored, which is harmless for Orion's belt (under 0.1 degrees over 12,000 years) but not for near, fast stars: Arcturus is off by about 8 degrees at 10,500 BC and Sirius by about 4.

items.title: Two more Orion checks: the kink, and the mirror
items.body: The Orion Correlation says Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure repeat Alnitak, Alnilam and Mintaka. Beyond the tilt check in the Contested lens, these are three numbers anyone can recompute. Both patterns are three nearly equally spaced points with a slight kink, but the kinks differ: the belt bends 7.5 degrees off straight at Alnilam, the pyramids about 12.5 degrees at Khafre. The pyramid coordinates are rounded to the arcsecond, which moves that bend by several degrees (95 per cent of random roundings land between 163 and 172), and the belt's value is reached in only about 2 per cent of them, so the pyramids' kink really does look sharper. Each published coordinate may also point at a slightly different spot on its pyramid, so read this as a hint of a mismatch, not a measurement of one. Two more checks: the belt's two gaps differ by 2 per cent where the pyramids' differ by 0.1 per cent, and the kinks bend in opposite senses if both are drawn with east to the right, so the correlation needs the sky mirrored, east to the left as you see it looking south.
